creator: Alexander Terp
description:
`print("{")` is a syntax error. It shouldn't be - there is no interpolation there to fail at.

```
print("{")     ->  error[RAD10009]: Unexpected '"{"'
print("{}")    ->  error[RAD10001]: Expected identifier
print("{ }")   ->  error[RAD10001]: Expected identifier
```

**Recommended rule, and the reason it is narrow.** Treat `{` as a literal only where it *cannot* open an interpolation: immediately followed by the string terminator, or containing nothing but whitespace. Everything else keeps erroring.

The tempting wider rule - fall back to literal whenever the interpolation fails to parse - is a trap. `print("{name")` is a forgotten closing brace. Under the wider rule it silently prints `{name`, which converts a loud parse error into #153's own Tier 1 category. `{` followed by an identifier should stay an error precisely because it looks like an interpolation someone didn't finish.

Cases this fixes, all from #153:

| Case | Today | After |
|---|---|---|
| `print("{")` | error | prints `{` |
| `t.starts_with("{")` | error | works |
| `` `\.+*?()[]{}\|^$` `` | error | works, the pair is empty |
| `print("{name")` | error | error, unchanged and deliberate |
| `print("\d{4}")` | prints `\d4` | unchanged - see the constant-literal lint card in p0-tier1 |

**`{{` was considered and is not recommended.** It doesn't work today (`print("{{")` errors), `\{` already does the job and is documented at `SYNTAX.md:913`, and for brace-dense text `r"..."` beats both. Adding `{{` gives two escapes for one job.

**The finding underneath this.** `\{` works and is documented, and the author reached for `r`-strings twice without finding it. The escape isn't the gap - discovery is. That is the sibling card in this column, and it stays worth doing for the cases that remain errors after this one lands.

Marked needs-decision because it changes what the grammar accepts. The recommendation above is the proposal, not a settled call.

---

### Orientation
- The grammar lives in the separate `tree-sitter-rad` repo, checked out at `~/src/tree-sitter-rad`. Interpolation is a grammar-level construct, so this change likely starts there rather than in this repo.
- `rts/` wraps that grammar and converts the CST to the AST in `rts/rl/`. `core/` then evaluates.
- Per AGENTS.md, iterate on the grammar with a temporary `replace github.com/amterp/tree-sitter-rad => <local path>` in go.mod, and remove it before committing - `./dev --release` refuses to release with one present.

### Where to start
- Confirm first whether this is fixable in the grammar or needs handling at CST-to-AST conversion. Read the interpolation rule in the tree-sitter-rad grammar before choosing.
- `rts/test/st_snapshots/` holds syntax-tree snapshots and will show exactly how the parse changes.

### How to verify
- `make build`, then `./bin/radd` over scratch scripts for every row of the table above, including the negative cases that must keep erroring.
- Syntax-tree snapshots: `go test ./rts -run TestSTSnapshots -update=<path substring>`.
- End-to-end: `core/testing/snapshots/` - look for the existing string-lexing cases, e.g. `-update=types/str_lexing`.
- Formatter round-trip: a literal brace must survive `rad fmt` unchanged. `rts/radfmt/snapshots/`.
- Editor path: `radls/lstesting/snapshots/` - highlighting should not mark a literal brace as an interpolation.

### Done when
- The three literal forms parse and print their braces.
- `print("{name")` still errors, with the improved message from the sibling card.
- All five snapshot suites updated and reviewed by diff.
- `SYNTAX.md` updated - it currently documents `\{` as the only answer.
- If the grammar changed: the tree-sitter-rad change is committed and tagged upstream, the go.mod `replace` is gone, and `make verify-generated` passes.

### Watch out for
Grammar changes ripple into all five snapshot suites plus the VS Code extension's highlighting. Scope creep risk: it is tempting to also "fix" `"\d{4}"` here. Don't - that is a valid interpolation, and it belongs to the lint card in p0-tier1.
title: Let an unambiguous literal brace parse
